newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish government starts education revenue drive.
newsitem.headline: Turkish government starts education revenue drive.

text.p: The Turkish government on Tuesday received the first cash from a wide range of price rises ostensibly earmarked for education reform, but which critics say will fuel inflation and may be diverted to other government spending.
The funds are scheduled to finance the ambitious expansion of secular education approved by parliament at the weekend.
The cash-raising drive has drawn fire even from the secular camp which backs the government and its plan to rein in Moslem religious education.
Education Minister Hikmet Ulugbay on Tuesday accepted a cheque for 100 billion Turkish lira ($600,000) skimmed from sales of national lottery tickets, Anatolian news agency said.
A package of price rises introduced last week included taxes on gambling, air tickets, beer and cigarettes, mobile phones, some stock market deals, and on gun and hunting permits.

The secular government says the revenues will go to finance an extension of compulsory education from the current five years to eight, a change that will effectively close religious schools at the expense of the government's Islamist political rivals.
The Islamist Welfare Party, forced out of office in June after months of pressure from the secular establishment and military, fiercely opposed the education reform bill.
Deputies from Welfare fought the bill's passage through parliament, filibustering late into the night in an unsuccessful bid to stop it becoming law.
The government estimates the cost of new schools, teachers, equipment and dormitories will add up to 668 trillion lira ($4.07 billion).

Handing over the first cheque, State Minister Eyup Asik said taxes on alcohol and cigarettes would bring in 1.2 trillion lira every week. "This is enough to open 10 to 15 schools a week," Anatolian quoted him as saying.

But many, even in the secular media which backs the current government, have complained about the possible inf lationary effects of the increases and fear Prime Minister Mesut Yilmaz may attempt to use some of the revenue for other purposes.
"Education is just an excuse. The aim is to close the budget deficit," Professor Oguz Oyan wrote in the passionately secular Cumhuriyet newspaper.
Turkey's annual inflation rate is around 80 percent. ($1 = 164,000 lira)
